vz_gauge_1u_application_the_size_of_most: 1U application — the size of most hits in the game — lands as 0.8U after the ×0.8 aura tax, then decays out over 2.5 × 1 + 7 = **9.5s**.
vz_gauge_re_applying_the_same_element_ex: Re-applying the same element (except Pyro, as of version 3.0) tops the gauge up but keeps the **first** application’s decay rate. 2U onto a 1U aura refills it and still drains at the slow 1U rate.
vz_gauge_since_version_3_0_pyro_doesn_t_: Since version 3.0, Pyro doesn’t top up. A hit weaker than the aura left on the target does nothing; one at least as strong replaces it, decay rate included. Here the 1U hit at 1s is too weak, and the one at 7s takes over and drains at the 1U rate.
vz_gauge_hydro_on_pyro_is_the_strong_dir: Hydro on Pyro is the strong direction: the trigger removes twice its own gauge. A single 1U Hydro hit clears a 2U Pyro aura outright — which is why one Vaporize usually leaves nothing behind.
vz_gauge_cryo_on_pyro_is_the_weak_direct: Cryo on Pyro is the weak direction: the trigger removes only **half** its own gauge, so each 1U hit chips 0.5U off a 2U aura instead of clearing it. (The ×1.5 on the chart is the **damage** multiplier — a different number from what the reaction costs the aura.)
vz_gauge_hydro_and_electro_coexist_and_e: Hydro and Electro coexist, and each tick drains 0.4U from **both** gauges. The smaller aura runs out first, which ends the reaction and leaves the larger one on the target. A 2U Hydro aura outlives a 1U Electro one.
vz_gauge_quicken_forms_1_1_and_lives_5_g: Quicken forms 1:1 and lives 5 × gauge + 6s. Aggravate hits on it consume nothing — but the same hit can re-Quicken off leftover Dendro. This example uses a starting 1.5U of Dendro — the strength of Nahida’s Tri-Karma Purification hits.
vz_gauge_one_pyro_hit_on_an_electro_char: One Pyro hit on an Electro-Charged target reacts with the Electro first (Overloaded); whatever gauge it has left then reacts with the Hydro (Vaporize).
vz_gauge_frozen_forms_at_2_min_aura_trig: Frozen forms at 2 × min(aura, trigger) and decays on its own accelerating clock. Any leftover Hydro keeps ticking down underneath it.
vz_gauge_pyro_melts_frozen_at_2_just_as_: Pyro melts Frozen at ×2, just as it melts Cryo. The game refuses Vaporize while any Frozen remains, so the Hydro underneath survives a hit that would have cleared it on a bare target.
vz_gauge_anemo_consumes_at_0_5_and_can_n: Anemo consumes at ×0.5 and can never attach as an aura — it takes half a unit and leaves the rest behind.
vz_gauge_geo_consumes_at_0_5_with_a_1s_r: Geo consumes at ×0.5 with a 1s reaction cooldown — the attempt inside the window is blocked and takes no gauge at all.
vz_gauge_hydro_on_dendro_is_the_weak_dir: Hydro on Dendro is the weak direction of Bloom: a 1U Hydro trigger removes only 0.5U of Dendro and spawns a Dendro Core, leaving the rest of the aura behind.
vz_gauge_burning_a_fixed_2u_aura_plus_a_: Burning = a fixed 2U aura plus a hidden fuel gauge that drains at 0.4U per second or faster. It deals damage every 0.25s and re-applies 1U Pyro about every 2s, until the fuel runs out. Feeding it more Dendro extends the burn.

faq_questions_about_the_site_as_a_whole_: Questions about the site as a whole. Each tool has its own chapter alongside this one.
faq_no_it_s_an_unofficial_fan_project_no: No. It’s an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by HoYoverse. It’s also not created or backed by any company. This is a solo dev project.
faq_what_does_the_beta_tag_mean: What does the beta tag mean?
faq_that_the_site_is_still_in_its_early: That the site is still in its early stages and could use some help. The {#beta}Beta{/beta} page goes into a little more detail.
faq_no_everything_you_set_up_your_profil: No. Everything you set up (your profiles with their rosters, teams, rotations, and lineups, and your settings) is stored in this browser and nowhere else. {#privacy}Privacy{/privacy} lists exactly what is kept in your browser and what leaves it. Because nothing is kept anywhere else, clearing this site’s data in your browser erases it, so it’s worth downloading a backup now and then.
faq_how_do_i_move_my_data_to_another_dev: How do I move my data to another device?
faq_in_settings_under_backup_click_expor: In {#settings}Settings{/settings} under {#strong}Backup{/strong}, click {#strong}Export…{/strong} to download all your data as one file. Move that file to the other device, then look for {#strong}Restore{/strong} and the {#strong}Import…{/strong} button to load that file’s data. The file carries every profile in this browser, each with its roster, teams, rotations, and lineups, plus your settings and the visualizers’ layout.
faq_what_does_a_share_link_carry: What does a share link carry?
faq_only_the_thing_you_re_sharing_writte: Only the thing you’re sharing, written into the link itself. A rotation planner link holds the notation and each character’s constellation and loadout; a team builder link holds the lineup’s teams and their constellations, but not their pinned rotations; a visualizers link holds that one instrument’s settings.
faq_a_link_opens_at_the_reader_s_own: A link opens at the reader’s own settings, not yours. If you share a rotation with Human timing on and they have it off, they see the frame-perfect version. Links can get long, and some chat apps cut them short; if one won’t open, that’s the usual cause.
faq_where_does_the_character_data_come_f: Where does the character data come from?
faq_each_kit_starts_from_genshin_db_s: Each kit starts from genshin-db’s datamine and is curated by hand: effects and conditions from the kit text, frame counts measured against gcsim wherever it has the character. Kits newer than genshin-db’s text are read from the Fandom wiki’s tooltips. {#about}About{/about} gives the full list of sources behind this project.
faq_the_coverage_page_answers_that_for_e: The {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage} answers that for every character, ability by ability, and gives the reason for anything the rotation planner leaves out. A character without curated frames still appears everywhere, marked “Not yet curated”, with generic frame timings as a stand-in.
faq_please_report_it_through_the_feedbac: Please report it through the {#feedback}feedback form{/feedback}. {#strong}Report a problem{/strong} in the top bar’s {#strong}?{/strong} menu opens the same form with a link to what you’re looking at already filled in. A character’s details card has its own link: {#strong}Something not right with this character?{/strong}
faq_why_is_the_timeline_faster_or_slower: Why is the timeline faster or slower than the timing I know?
faq_check_human_timing_it_s_on_by_defaul: Check {#strong}Human timing{/strong} (it’s on by default). This pads every input the game doesn’t buffer with a few frames of reaction time — 10 to start with, which is the KQM starting point. Normal attack into normal attack is queued up by the game, so no padding is added there. Turn it off in {#settings}Settings{/settings} to see the frame-perfect rotation, or tune it there.
faq_swapping_characters_costs_time_eithe: Swapping characters costs time either way. Swaps are calculated as your ping plus about 90 ms. At critcalc’s default ping setting (60 ms), that results in nine frames for every swap. Set your own ping under {#strong}Swap ping{/strong} in Settings.
faq_why_does_a_skill_come_back_later_tha: Why does a skill come back later than its cooldown says?
faq_because_for_most_skills_the_cooldown: Because for most skills the cooldown doesn’t start on the button press. It starts a few frames into the cast (eleven frames for Nahida’s skill, for example), and the timeline draws it from there. A few skills start even later: Xilonen’s cooldown timer only begins once her Nightsoul state ends, so it runs after the stance rather than from the cast.
faq_keqing_mains_its_notation_for_rotati: {#kqm}Keqing Mains{/kqm}: its notation for rotations, its names for mechanics, and the game’s own names for reactions — Frozen and Overloaded, for instance.
faq_does_it_work_on_a_phone: Does it work on a phone?
faq_yes_down_to_320px_wide_though_the: Yes, down to 320px wide, though the rotation planner and team builder are easier with more room. On a phone the rotation planner starts with the Buffs and Auras layers off, and you can hide the bench.
faq_if_you_use_critcalc_on_your_phone_of: If you use critcalc on your phone often, I’d suggest adding it to your home screen, which opens the site without your browser’s bars. On an iPhone, it also stops Safari from clearing your data when you haven’t visited in a while. It still needs a connection: Character data loads as you use it, so going offline partway through can leave a character half-loaded.
faq_here_s_how_to_add_it_to_your_home_sc: Here’s how to add it to your home screen on an {#android}Android phone (Chrome){/android} and on an {#iphone}iPhone (Safari){/iphone}.
help_planner_a_ledger_of_where_every_sta: A ledger of where every star will be, frame by frame. Its compiler held that the heavens keep perfect time and can be charted in intricate detail.
help_planner_write_a_rotation_in_kqm_not: Write a rotation in KQM notation and the rotation planner draws it as a timeline: who is on field, every cast and its cooldown, the buffs it grants, and what it does to the enemy’s aura, timed from measured frame data.
help_planner_the_composer_under_the_time: The composer under the timeline takes {#kqm}KQM notation{/kqm}. A rotation is segments separated by {#code}>{/code}, each starting with a character’s name and followed by what they do:
help_planner_n_to_n9_are_normal_attacks_: {#code}N{/code} to {#code}N9{/code} are normal attacks — {#code}N3{/code} is three swings, and {#code}N2 N3{/code} continues the same string. {#code}C{/code} is a charged attack, {#code}P{/code} a plunge ({#code}lP{/code} a low one), {#code}D{/code} a dash, and {#code}J{/code} a jump. {#code}A{/code} is a bow’s fully charged aimed shot.
help_planner_e_and_q_are_skill_and_burst: {#code}E{/code} and {#code}Q{/code} are skill and burst, with {#code}hE{/code} for a hold where the kit has one.
help_planner_stances_add_special_forms_s: Stances add special forms: {#code}sE{/code} a special skill, {#code}sQ{/code} a short burst, {#code}sC{/code} a special charged attack, and {#code}F{/code} the finisher of a spinning charged attack like Mavuika’s.
help_planner_3_n2_d_or_n2_d_x3_repeat_th: {#code}3[N2 D]{/code} or {#code}[N2 D]x3{/code} repeat the actions in the brackets, {#code}(E){/code} marks an optional action that isn’t drawn on the timeline, and {#code}E/Q{/code} draws the first of two alternatives.
help_planner_critcalc_adds_a_time_token_: critcalc adds a time token of its own, written {#code}~Xs{/code}. {#code}~1.5s{/code} adds 1.5 seconds of waiting on the active character’s row. A few abilities take it as their length instead:
help_planner_mizuki_s_dreamdrifter_and_c: {#strong}Mizuki’s Dreamdrifter and Chasca’s Spirit Reins, Shadow Hunt{/strong} run their full length unless {#code}~Xs{/code} is the last thing in that character’s turn. {#code}Mizuki E ~2s{/code} ends Dreamdrifter after two seconds, so a swap can land at that moment.
help_planner_sandrone_s_charged_attack_h: {#strong}Sandrone’s Charged Attack{/strong} holds until just before Fagio overheats (reaches maximum Decoding Power). {#code}C ~1.5s{/code} holds for 1.5 seconds instead, regardless of the current Decoding Power level.
help_planner_sayu_s_held_skill_rolls_for: {#strong}Sayu’s held Skill{/strong} rolls for as long as you set with {#code}hE ~2s{/code}, up to ten seconds.
help_planner_neuvillette_s_charged_attac: {#strong}Neuvillette’s Charged Attack{/strong} runs the full beam. {#code}C ~1s{/code} ends it early, at its last hit by then.
help_planner_names_are_the_game_s_displa: Names are the game’s display names — Kazuha, Raiden, Tartaglia — and the composer suggests them as you type. Actions can be run together ({#code}QEN2{/code}), and pasted rotations are cleaned up for you: footnote marks dropped, line breaks joined.
help_planner_undo_and_redo_sit_at_the_en: Undo and redo sit at the end of the composer, alongside Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Shift+Z (⌘Z and ⌘⇧Z on a Mac). They work for edits made from the bench and the team builder too. Each rotation keeps its own edit history until the page reloads.
help_planner_a_skill_or_burst_written_be: A skill or burst written before it’s ready waits for its cooldown, and everything after it waits too. Charges come back one at a time, as in the game.
help_planner_the_composer_holding_a_rota: The composer holding a rotation: Sucrose’s hE underlined in yellow, and Flinz, a misspelled name, underlined in orange.
help_planner_the_composer_underlines_wha: The composer underlines what it can’t draw exactly as written, in two colors. An {#strong}orange{/strong} underline means it couldn’t take the text: a name that matches no character, like {#warn}Flinz{/warn} (that segment is skipped), an aimed shot on a character without a bow, or a token it doesn’t know. A {#strong}yellow{/strong} one means it took the text and drew a stand-in: a hold version the kit doesn’t have, like {#approx}hE{/approx}, timed as a tap instead; a plunge with no measured frames; a fifth character, who has no slot. Hover the token for the reason.
help_planner_walk_cancels_w_ends_the_att: {#strong}Walk-cancels.{/strong} {#code}W{/code} ends the attack string the way walking does in game: {#code}N1 W N1{/code} is two first hits. For most attacks a walk can start only once the animation has ended, though some characters can walk out a little sooner. Regardless, walk cancels give you a reset of the attack string without the stamina a dash would cost.
help_planner_the_bench_holds_four_slots_: The bench holds four slots. Typing a character’s name puts them in the first empty slot, even with no actions after it, and deleting all of their notation frees the slot again. A team opened from the Library, a lineup, or a team link is placed in its slots and stays there while you write. When a placed character isn’t written into the notation yet, they’re shown resting (dimmed). When no slot is empty, any other name you type takes the first resting character’s slot.
help_planner_flins_s_bench_card_its_five: Flins’s bench card, its five controls numbered.
help_planner_each_slot_on_the_bench_besi: Each slot on the bench beside the timeline has a bench card. Clicking the portrait {#ref}1{/ref} opens the character’s page in the inspector. On a wide screen, the two buttons at the card’s left change the slot: The top one {#ref}2{/ref} opens the team builder’s swap mode for that slot, and picking someone there takes you back to the planner with the notation renamed throughout. The bottom one {#ref}3{/ref} removes the character from the team and deletes their notation. Clicking an empty slot’s portrait adds someone instead. On a phone, {#strong}Remove from team{/strong} is on the character’s page in the inspector.
help_planner_the_chip_on_the_portrait_is: The chip on the portrait {#ref}4{/ref} is the character’s constellation, and the pill beside it {#ref}5{/ref} sets their weapon and artifact set for this rotation. A character you own is at your roster’s level. Choosing another level for them makes a what-if: a copy of the rotation in Theorycraft at that level, paired with this one so you can switch between the two. A character you don’t own keeps the level this rotation gives them, and their chip is drawn hollow. In Theorycraft every level belongs to the rotation.
help_planner_a_character_without_curated: A character without curated frame data carries a mark beside their name, and their actions are drawn with generic timing. The {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage} shows what is covered for each character.
help_planner_type_blank_in_the_notation_: Type “Blank” in the notation box to create a stand-in for a character the planner doesn’t have, such as one you’re theorycrafting before release. Write it like any other character: {#code}Blank E N3 Q{/code}.
help_planner_to_show_how_long_a_skill_or: To show how long a skill or burst lasts, put the length in braces right after it: {#code}Blank E\{8s\}{/code} draws an 8-second bar, and {#code}Q\{12s\}{/code} a 12-second one. Blank has no cooldowns, so casting an ability again right away ends the bar before it. Please note that Blank’s ability durations are left out of the KQM notation export.
help_planner_a_rotation_can_only_use_one: A rotation can only use one Blank (if you would like support for more than one Blank, please {#feedback}request it{/feedback}). Its actions use generic timing, and none of them hit, grant a buff, or apply an element.
help_planner_blank_counts_as_no_element_: Blank counts as no element. It never breaks a rule like Nilou’s (no Pyro, Cryo, Electro, Anemo, or Geo teammates), but it can’t supply an element a teammate needs either, like the Electro member Chevreuse looks for.
help_planner_columbina_s_rows_over_the_f: Columbina’s rows over the first five seconds: her skill and its cooldown, two summons, her burst, her active row, and the swap connector down to Ineffa, numbered.
help_planner_each_character_gets_a_group: Each character gets a group of rows: their skill {#ref}1{/ref}, then any summons and shields {#ref}2{/ref}, then their burst {#ref}3{/ref}, then the active row {#ref}4{/ref}, which shows when they’re on field and what they’re doing. Received buffs and weapon procs follow underneath, and connectors mark each swap {#ref}5{/ref}.
help_planner_a_skill_or_burst_bar_is_fol: A skill or burst bar is followed by a faded tail {#ref}6{/ref} labeled with the cooldown, ending where the ability can be used again. A stance that lasts longer than its own cooldown is drawn dimmer past the point where the cooldown ran out.
help_planner_below_the_characters_are_th: Below the characters are the team-wide lanes — team buffs, Nightsoul bursts, and Moonsign’s Ascendant Gleam bonuses when the team has them — and above the composer a strip lists the always-on bonuses: resonances, faction bonuses, and permanent passives.
help_planner_energy_isn_t_modeled_a_burs: Energy isn’t modeled: A burst is ready whenever its cooldown is.
help_planner_zoom_in_the_toolbar_opens_a: {#strong}Zoom{/strong} in the toolbar opens a slider and {#strong}Reset{/strong}; the mouse wheel over the ruler scrolls sideways. {#strong}Total{/strong} is the rotation’s length.
help_planner_buffs_and_auras_in_the_tool: {#strong}Buffs{/strong} and {#strong}Auras{/strong} in the toolbar are layers. Buffs hides every bar that says what a cast grants — buff rows, weapon procs, the team lanes, and the always-on strip — and Auras hides the aura lane. Skills, bursts, summons, and shields stay, since they say when an ability is happening. With both off, the timeline is ability timings and nothing else. If you change either one, your choice is remembered. On a small screen both are off to begin with.
help_planner_human_timing_is_on_by_defau: {#strong}Human timing{/strong} is on by default. It adds some frames of reaction time before each input the game doesn’t buffer for you: after a skill, burst, plunge, dash, or jump, from a normal attack into anything but another normal or a charged attack, and on the first input after a swap. Normal into normal and normal into charged are exempt, because the game allows queuing of those inputs. A bow’s charged shot is the exception: It always takes the reaction time.
help_planner_flins_s_active_row_with_a_h: Flins’s active row, with a hatched sliver of reaction time before each input after his swap in, one of them numbered.
help_planner_settings_decides_what_it_ch: Settings decides what it changes. {#strong}Padding{/strong} (the default) is the reaction time. This is 10 frames to start with (the KQM starting point), and you can adjust it there. {#strong}Animations{/strong} lets each action play out in full instead of canceling. {#strong}Both{/strong} enables both. The padding shows as hatched slivers {#ref}1{/ref} on the active row, which {#strong}Mark padding{/strong} turns off. Turn Human timing off in Settings to see the frame-perfect rotation. While it’s on, a {#strong}Human timing{/strong} tag beside {#strong}Total{/strong} says so and opens Settings.
help_planner_swaps_take_time_either_way_: Swaps take time either way: your ping plus about 90 ms, set under {#strong}Swap ping{/strong} in Settings. If you write the same character on both sides of a {#code}>{/code} it costs no swap time, since the character never left the field. Laps relies on this when a rotation ends with the character it starts with.
help_planner_a_swap_ends_a_stance_only_w: A swap ends a stance only where the game does: Hu Tao’s Paramita ends when she leaves, while Mavuika’s Nightsoul Blessing or Noelle’s Sweeping Time carries on. A few stances hold the field — Mizuki’s Dreamdrifter keeps her on field until it ends, unless the segment is cut short with a time token or a second press of her skill.
help_planner_because_human_timing_is_you: Because Human timing is your preference, it isn’t stored in a share link. Someone opening your rotation sees it at their own setting.
help_planner_the_playback_controls_with_: The playback controls with Laps on, and the timeline zoomed out: the cursor partway through the first lap and the gold mark where the second begins, numbered.
help_planner_play_or_space_runs_a_cursor: {#strong}Play{/strong} {#ref}1{/ref} (or Space) runs a cursor {#ref}2{/ref} along the timeline at game speed, and the plate {#ref}3{/ref} beside it slows it to 0.75× or 0.5×. With sound on, you’ll hear four beats to count you in, then a note for every input. Settings has the sounds and the volume. {#strong}Back to the start{/strong} (Home) rewinds.
help_planner_bluetooth_headphones_and_sp: Bluetooth headphones and speakers delay sound by a tenth of a second or more, so the cursor waits for your device’s delay and stays in step with what you hear.
help_planner_laps_simulates_the_rotation: {#strong}Laps{/strong} {#ref}4{/ref} simulates the rotation five times in a row, as one run. A skill still on cooldown waits and pushes the rest back, and buffs, stacks, and auras carry from one lap into the next, so a rotation that doesn’t loop cleanly shows it. Gold marks {#ref}5{/ref} on the ruler show where each lap begins. Laps isn’t saved, shared, or exported.
help_planner_the_aura_lane_over_the_firs: The aura lane over the first seven seconds: Hydro and then Electro gauge lines, their element pills, the Lunar-Charged marker, and a Thundercloud below the baseline, numbered.
help_planner_the_aura_lane_above_the_rul: The aura lane above the ruler represents the elemental aura on the enemy. The gauge lines {#ref}1{/ref} draw each element attached to them, and a line’s height is how much gauge is left, so you can see an aura land, decay, get topped up, and get eaten by a reaction. The gaps are where the next trigger has nothing to react with. Hover anywhere on it to read all the auras present at that moment.
help_planner_above_the_lines_a_pill_in_t: Above the lines, a pill {#ref}2{/ref} in the element’s color marks each hit that applied an element, and a labeled marker {#ref}3{/ref} above that names each reaction it caused. A run of a ticking reaction such as Electro-Charged is one marker with a count. Frozen, Quicken, Burning, and Burning’s Dendro fuel are separate objects from the auras that made them, with their own decay, so they get their own lines. A yellow ring on a pill means the hit has no measured gauge strength, and 1U is assumed.
help_planner_the_reaction_spawns_below_t: {#strong}The reaction spawns{/strong} {#ref}4{/ref}, below the baseline, are what some reactions leave behind: a Dendro Core from Bloom, a Starlight Prism from Stellar-Conduct, a Thundercloud from Lunar-Charged, and Moondrifts from Lunar-Crystallize. A dot marks each one appearing, and a stepped shape shows how many there are, so a step down is one expiring or being spent. A Dendro Core arrives half a second after its Bloom, lasts 6s, and there can be five on the field at once. Hyperbloom or Burgeon takes the oldest Dendro Core. A Starlight Prism lasts 7s and a further Stellar-Conduct refreshes it. There is only ever one Thundercloud, lasting 5.5s, and another Lunar-Charged restarts its clock. Lunar-Crystallize keeps three Moondrifts topped up, 9s each, drawn as one row. The damage these deal isn’t modeled; their presence is, along with any character effect that depends on it.
help_planner_the_polestar_field_a_starli: {#strong}The Polestar Field.{/strong} A Starlight Prism holds a Polestar Field around it, and the field’s buffs sit in the team buffs, because any party member’s Stellar-Conduct raises the same field. Its Cryo and Electro bonus moves: The field counts the Cryo and Electro hits that applied an element, resets every 4s, and boosts based on that count — 20% with none, 29% at one, up to 40% at twelve.
help_planner_log_in_the_toolbar_opens_th: {#strong}Log{/strong} in the toolbar opens the aura log beside the timeline. Hovering a row highlights that moment on the aura lane, clicking one scrolls there, and clicking a pill or marker on the aura lane opens the log at its row. The log also works with the Auras layer off.
help_planner_the_model_behind_it_is_the_: The model behind it is the gauge explorer’s: the ×0.8 aura tax, decay rates, how much each reaction consumes, and the Crystallize cooldown. It assumes one enemy without a permanent aura that applies nothing back to you, and Shatter isn’t modeled. (If you would like to see permanent auras as a feature, please send a request through the {#feedback}feedback form{/feedback}.)
help_planner_the_inspector_open_on_the_t: The inspector open on the team: Columbina’s caveats for her normal attack, skill, and burst, then Ineffa, then Sucrose’s.
help_planner_inspector_opens_a_panel_bes: {#strong}Inspector{/strong} opens a panel beside the timeline. It starts on the team: each character with the caveats on their kit, where the timeline knowingly differs from the game, with constellation notes from the level the rotation uses. Click a bench portrait, a buff bar, an E or Q, a summon or shield, or a chip under the chart, and the inspector shows that instead. Clicking the same thing again closes it. A character’s page links to their coverage.
help_planner_turn_on_coverage_strips_in_: Turn on {#strong}Coverage strips{/strong} in Settings to draw each character’s coverage under the composer and dim the parts of the kit this rotation doesn’t use.
help_planner_the_planner_shows_one_rotat: The planner shows one rotation at a time and saves it as you work, in the profile you’re in. The rotation’s name in the top bar opens {#strong}Rotations{/strong} in the Library, where {#strong}New rotation{/strong} starts another and each one can be pinned, renamed, or deleted.
help_planner_a_rotation_in_theorycraft_c: A rotation in Theorycraft can go to one of your profiles with {#strong}Move to a profile{/strong}. Before it moves, you see which levels change, since the profile’s roster decides them for characters you own.
help_planner_compare_under_the_bench_pai: {#strong}Compare{/strong}, under the bench, pairs two rotations. {#strong}Duplicate and compare{/strong} copies this one so you can change the copy, and {#strong}Compare with…{/strong} picks another from the Library. The button that takes Compare’s place, or ⌃`, switches between them.
help_planner_share_in_the_toolbar_copies: {#strong}Share{/strong} in the toolbar copies a link, the KQM notation, or an image of the timeline. The link opens the rotation with its constellations and loadouts in Theorycraft, so it doesn’t change the reader’s profiles. The KQM copy removes inputs that are specific to critcalc — time tokens, optional marks, and stack counts — and keeps the rest as you wrote it. The image is the whole timeline, not only the part on screen, with the notation written above it.
help_planner_the_rotation_planner_on_a_p: The rotation planner on a phone: the bench as a row above the timeline, and the composer open at the foot of the screen with its row of keys.
help_planner_on_a_phone_the_composer_doc: On a phone the composer {#ref}1{/ref} docks to the bottom of the screen. Collapsed it shows the last line of the rotation. Tap it to open it with the keyboard, and tap anywhere else to close it. A row of keys {#ref}2{/ref} above the keyboard offers the inputs that fit where the cursor is.
help_planner_the_bench_becomes_a_row_abo: The bench becomes a row {#ref}3{/ref} above the timeline. The arrow at the left end of the strip above it folds the row away. Tapping a portrait on a phone opens the character’s details. The Buffs and Auras layers are turned off by default and the zoom starts wider than on desktop.
help_tb_a_brass_disc_of_nested_rings_eac: A brass disc of nested rings, each engraved with names. Turning four into alignment can answer many questions, or raise new ones.
help_tb_a_party_setup_screen_build_a_lin: A party setup screen. Build a lineup of teams for Stygian Onslaught, the Spiral Abyss, or anything else, and each team shows what it can provide at the constellations it uses. For Imaginarium Theater, build a cast and see which difficulty your roster can enter.
help_tb_the_new_lineup_menu_open_offerin: The New lineup menu open, offering Stygian Onslaught, Spiral Abyss, Imaginarium Theater, and Custom.
help_tb_new_lineup_in_the_library_under_: {#strong}New lineup{/strong}, in the Library under {#strong}Lineups{/strong}, starts a lineup in one of four shapes:
help_tb_stygian_onslaught_three_teams_on: {#strong}Stygian Onslaught{/strong}: three teams, one per battlefield, each with its boss and the season’s checks.
help_tb_spiral_abyss_two_teams_for_floor: {#strong}Spiral Abyss{/strong}: two teams for Floor 12’s first and second half. While a current cycle is live, each half shows its blessing and {#strong}Opponents{/strong} list.
help_tb_imaginarium_theater_a_cast_inste: {#strong}Imaginarium Theater{/strong}: a cast instead of teams, for the month’s season (see {#theater}Imaginarium Theater{/theater} below).
help_tb_custom_one_team_to_start_and_add: {#strong}Custom{/strong}: one team to start, and {#strong}Add team{/strong} in the toolbar for more, up to twelve.
help_tb_new_lineup_on_a_team_in_teams_do: {#strong}New lineup{/strong} on a team in {#strong}Teams{/strong} does the same, and the lineup starts with that team. The builder shows one lineup at a time and saves it as you work. The lineup’s name in the top bar opens {#strong}Lineups{/strong}, where each one can be pinned, renamed, or deleted.
help_tb_once_you_ve_added_characters_to_: Once you’ve added characters to a lineup, it’s pinned to the endgame cycle you were planning for at that time. Once a new cycle is released, you can open your existing lineup and use the dropdown at the top to select the most recent cycle, or you can simply create a new lineup to keep your previous endgame lineups archived. Empty Stygian and Abyss lineups that you haven’t touched automatically update to the latest cycle.
help_tb_in_the_library_the_top_section_t: In the Library, the top section ({#strong}This cycle{/strong}) keeps all your lineups for endgame content that is still live. It also shows a blank card for any live endgame you haven’t made a lineup for yet.
help_tb_no_repeats_keeps_each_character_: {#strong}No repeats{/strong} keeps each character on one team, the way the game does. It is on for Stygian and Abyss lineups and off for Custom ones. While it’s on, picking someone who is already on another team takes them off it, and picking them again adds them here. You can turn it on or off on any lineup. You may want to turn it off if you are preparing for the Menacing or lower difficulty levels of Stygian Onslaught.
help_tb_the_characters_grid_under_a_bann: The Characters grid under a banner reading Adding to Team 2 · 3/4, with the magnifier showing on Zibai’s card.
help_tb_click_a_team_to_select_it_a_bann: Click a team to select it. A banner in the team’s color {#ref}1{/ref} says where your picks will go — “Adding to Team 2 · 3/4”. Clicking a character card puts them in the first empty slot; clicking them again takes them out and leaves the others where they are. With no team chosen, picks fill the first team that has room and move on once it’s full.
help_tb_the_magnifier_on_a_card_opens_th: The magnifier on a card {#ref}2{/ref} opens the character’s details: every capability with the ability that grants it, its constellation and any condition it needs, plus their cooldowns and Energy cost. Ownership is shown there but is edited in the Roster (see {#roster}below{/roster}).
help_tb_the_toolbar_and_filter_strip_ove: The toolbar and filter strip over the Characters grid, with Owned on, and the first row of cards.
help_tb_the_strip_over_characters_filter: The strip over {#strong}Characters{/strong} filters by role {#ref}1{/ref}, by element and by what a character can provide. Roles are filtered one at a time; elements match any of those you pick; capabilities under {#strong}Can provide{/strong} {#ref}2{/ref} match only characters who provide all of them. Choosing a role also sorts the grid into sections: Damage roles are sorted by element, while Support and Survivability roles are sorted by capability.
help_tb_character_roles_come_from_genshi: Character roles come from Genshin’s own classifications, used in the Imaginarium Theater. Every character is categorized as On-Field or Off-Field, and DPS, Support, or Survivability. We’ve only made two modifications to the in-game assignment: Fischl and Rosaria are additionally tagged as Support for the team buffs they provide.
help_tb_the_toolbar_narrows_further_a_na: The toolbar narrows further: a name search, {#strong}Owned{/strong} and {#strong}Wishlist{/strong}, and {#strong}More{/strong} for weapon, rarity, region, and factions like Hexerei or Moonsign.
help_tb_the_column_of_icons_on_a_card_is: The column of icons on a card is that character’s own capabilities. Each is lit {#ref}3{/ref} if it’s available at the constellations you’ve specified and dimmed {#ref}4{/ref} if it needs a higher one (hover over it to find out what would unlock it). The constellation lens in the toolbar {#ref}5{/ref} sets that level: C0 through C6, or {#strong}My constellations{/strong}, the default, which reads your roster. It changes the Characters grid only. A team reads your roster for characters you own and its own level for anyone else.
help_tb_some_kits_have_no_capability_dat: Some kits have no capability data yet. While you filter by capability they are listed separately under “Not yet curated”, because a missing icon there means unknown rather than no. The {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage} shows where each character currently stands.
help_tb_a_team_s_fifteen_capability_icon: A team’s fifteen capability icons, some lit with dots beneath them and some faint.
help_tb_each_team_shows_fifteen_capabili: Each team shows fifteen capabilities in three groups: survival (healing, shields, cleanse, taunt), support (buffs, energy, RES shred, grouping, infusion, interruption RES) and off-field damage. A lit icon means someone on the team provides it, with a dot for each provider {#ref}1{/ref}. A faint icon means nobody does {#ref}2{/ref}. Dots on a faint icon are characters who would provide that at a higher constellation or on a different team {#ref}3{/ref}.
help_tb_conditions_are_read_against_the_: Conditions are read against the team. A buff that needs a Pyro-affected enemy lights only if someone applies Pyro, and a buff that is conditional on team composition only lights up when the condition is met. Adding a character can change a teammate’s capabilities this way, which is easiest to see by hovering a card with your cursor: The selected team previews how its capabilities would change with the character in focus.
help_tb_click_a_faint_capability_to_find: Click a faint capability to find who provides it. The Characters grid narrows to that capability and that team becomes the destination for your next pick.
help_tb_the_icons_say_what_a_team_can_do: The icons say what a team can do, not how much or how often — there are no amounts or uptimes here. The rotation planner is where you can test this out.
help_tb_on_a_stygian_battlefield_the_chi: On a Stygian battlefield, the chips beside the boss are that battlefield’s checks. A thumbs up marks something the battlefield favors and a thumbs down something the boss resists. Once a team is on it, a check mark means the team brings a favored thing, and a warning means it does something the boss resists. A few checks can’t be read from a team (how often you plunge, for instance) and are left without a verdict. The boss’s magnifier opens its HP and mechanics in the game’s words. Enemy RES isn’t shown; you can check {#stygian}Stygian.moe{/stygian} for a breakdown of elemental resistances during the different phases of the battle.
help_tb_swap_mode_replacing_columbina_fi: Swap mode replacing Columbina: five characters under Keeps everything and six under Trades, which lose DMG% buff, with a green Shield icon on Candace’s card.
help_tb_click_a_portrait_in_the_selected: Click a portrait in the selected team to replace that character. The banner {#ref}1{/ref} reads “Replacing Columbina”, and the Characters grid regroups by what the swap would do to the team:
help_tb_keeps_everything_nothing_the_tea: {#strong}Keeps everything{/strong}: Nothing the team provides is lost.
help_tb_trades_something_is_lost_listed_: {#strong}Trades{/strong}: Something is lost, listed in the section header {#ref}2{/ref}.
help_tb_changes_the_reactions_the_team_s: {#strong}Changes the reactions{/strong}: The team’s reactions or resonance change, whether or not it also loses something.
help_tb_not_yet_curated_no_capability_da: {#strong}Not yet curated{/strong}: no capability data, so the swap can’t be read.
help_tb_what_a_candidate_would_add_shows: What a candidate would add shows as green icons on their card {#ref}3{/ref}. Only characters who play the same position (on field or off) are offered at first; a button at the foot of the grid shows the rest. Escape or the banner’s ✕ leaves without swapping.
help_tb_picking_someone_makes_the_swap_a: Picking someone makes the swap, and the notice above the lineup offers to {#strong}Undo{/strong} it. If the team had a pinned rotation, the pin drops, because the rotation was written for the old character; the notice then offers to open a copy in the rotation planner with the new character written in their place.
help_tb_the_rotation_planner_sends_you_h: The rotation planner sends you here too: {#strong}⇄{/strong} on one of its bench cards opens swap mode for that slot. Picking someone renames them in the notation and takes you back; Cancel returns without changing anything. Clicking an empty slot’s portrait works the same way and adds someone instead.
help_tb_a_theater_lineup_is_a_cast_not_t: A Theater lineup is a cast, not teams. This will help you decide which difficulty level you can enter based on your roster, or think about which of your characters you want to enter into the Alternate Cast. Theater lineups open on the highest difficulty your roster can enter this month, but you can always choose a lower difficulty level using the dropdown menu.
help_tb_with_a_theater_lineup_open_the_c: With a Theater lineup open, the character grid switches to only displaying characters eligible to enter the Theater that month, including Special Guest Stars. The six Opening Characters are already entered into your lineup, so you won’t find them in the grid. The {#strong}Auto-select{/strong} button fills all of your available slots, starting with any Special Guest Stars you can enter and then choosing from your roster from most recent characters to oldest.
help_tb_1_supporting_cast_counts_a_frien: {#strong}+1 Supporting Cast{/strong} counts a friend’s character you plan to invite.
help_tb_the_roster_doesn_t_track_levels_: The roster doesn’t track levels. Mark anyone who can’t enter (in practice, below level 70) with {#strong}Can’t enter Theater{/strong} in the Roster’s edit mode, or press T, and they stay out of every Theater lineup.
help_tb_a_theater_lineup_has_no_share_bu: A Theater lineup has no {#strong}Share{/strong} button, since it is individual to each profile’s roster.
help_tb_if_this_profile_has_a_rotation_f: If this profile has a rotation for exactly the four characters in a team (in any order), you will see the pin under {#strong}Planner{/strong} become a menu, which you can use to pin a specific rotation to that team. Characters you don’t own then read that rotation’s constellations. {#strong}Planner{/strong} opens the pinned rotation, or, if nothing is pinned, a new rotation with the team already on the bench. Changing the team’s members drops the pin; the rotation itself stays in the Library.
help_tb_your_roster_is_under_roster_in_t: Your roster is under {#strong}Roster{/strong} in the profile menu (your picture in the top bar), and {#strong}Edit in Roster{/strong} in a character’s details goes there too. Mark who you own, who you’re wishing for, and at what constellation. {#strong}Owned{/strong}, {#strong}Wishlist{/strong}, {#strong}My constellations{/strong}, and the constellation chips all read it. In Theorycraft there is no roster: every character is there at every level.
help_tb_a_team_s_four_portraits_illuga_w: A team’s four portraits; Illuga, who isn’t owned, wears a hollow C6 chip.
help_tb_the_chip_on_a_team_portrait_is_t: The chip on a team portrait is the constellation that team uses. A character you own is at your roster’s level; the chip is hollow for a character you don’t own {#ref}1{/ref}.
help_tb_share_in_the_toolbar_copies_a_li: {#strong}Share{/strong} in the toolbar copies a link with the lineup’s teams, preset, season, No repeats setting, and constellations. (Pinned rotations are not included.) It opens in Theorycraft for the reader.
help_tb_the_builder_on_a_phone_showing_t: The builder on a phone showing the Lineup pane, with the Characters button above the first team.
help_tb_on_narrower_screens_characters_a: On narrower screens Characters and the Lineup are two panes with a button to switch between them {#ref}1{/ref}. Filling a team takes you to the Lineup, and choosing a slot to fill takes you to Characters. There is no hover preview on touch.
help_vz_a_dome_with_eight_apertures_each: A dome with eight apertures, each lens ground to bring a single principle of the expanse into focus.
help_vz_eight_instruments_each_taking_on: Eight instruments, each taking one mechanic and drawing it, with controls to push it around and a Readout that puts the result in words.
help_vz_the_gauge_explorer_s_bar_the_ins: The Gauge explorer’s bar: the instrument menu, then Defaults, Copy link, the ⋯ menu, and Layout.
help_vz_the_workspace_shows_one_instrume: The workspace shows one instrument at a time, picked from the menu at its top left {#ref}1{/ref}. {#strong}Layout{/strong} {#ref}2{/ref}, at the bar’s right end, shows two or three side by side when the window is wide enough, or {#strong}Auto{/strong} for as many as fit. Picking an instrument already showing in another tile swaps the two, and {#strong}Reset layout{/strong} goes back to one instrument and the default lineup.
help_vz_each_instrument_has_defaults_whi: Each instrument has {#strong}Defaults{/strong} {#ref}3{/ref}, which puts its controls back to their defaults (with Undo), and {#strong}Copy link{/strong} {#ref}4{/ref}, which copies a link that reopens the instrument exactly as it looks now (in the reader’s first tile). Its {#strong}⋯{/strong} menu {#ref}5{/ref} has {#strong}How it works{/strong}, which opens this page at the instrument’s section, and {#strong}Report a problem{/strong}, for feedback about that instrument.
help_vz_each_instrument_s_settings_are_s: Each instrument’s settings are saved with your profile, and the layout with this browser, so both are as you left them next visit. A link you open shows the settings it carries, and those are what’s kept from then on.
help_vz_the_crit_heatmap_with_a_build_at: The crit heatmap with a build at 50% CRIT Rate and 200% CRIT DMG on its 300 CV line, the best split ringed at 75% and 150%, a pinned build at 70% and 140%, and the bars for eight hits under the map.
help_vz_your_average_damage_per_hit_1_cr: Your average damage per hit, 1 + CRIT Rate × CRIT DMG, across every split of CRIT Rate (up the side) and CRIT DMG (along the bottom). Press anywhere on the map to move your build {#ref}1{/ref} there, or drag a handle on either axis, or type a value beside it. The right edge and the curves that extend from it reveal bands of average damage increase over many rotations.
help_vz_the_solid_line_through_your_buil: The solid line through your build is every build with your total crit value (CV), counted as 2 × CRIT Rate + CRIT DMG with base crit stats included. A ring {#ref}2{/ref} marks that budget’s best split, which sits on the 1:2 ratio until CRIT Rate would pass 100% and then leaves it; press it to move your build there. {#strong}Pin this build{/strong} holds a second marker {#ref}3{/ref}, and the line from it to yours shows how much the move changes your average.
help_vz_the_average_hides_how_uneven_a_r: The average hides how uneven a rotation can be. The bars beside the map (under it, on a phone) {#ref}4{/ref} share its CRIT Rate axis: one for each number of crits in a rotation, set at that number’s share of the hits, as long as its chance. Set the hits over the map. {#strong}No-crit shading{/strong} darkens builds by their chance of a whole rotation without a single crit, and {#strong}Roll{/strong} plays one rotation and lights the bar it lands on.
help_vz_i_came_up_with_the_concept_for_t: I came up with the concept for the crit heatmap and wondered how best to present it visually, and subsequently came across {#eod}EODGamer’s spreadsheet heatmap{/eod}. Thanks, EODGamer — your chart confirmed the shape in my mind.
help_vz_the_gauge_explorer_s_overvape_ex: The gauge explorer’s Overvape example: Hydro at 0s, Electro at 1s marked Electro-Charged, and Pyro at 2s marked Overloaded and Vaporize, with each aura’s curve dropping where the Pyro reacts.
help_vz_how_auras_attach_decay_and_get_c: How auras attach, decay and get consumed, over up to 15s and eight applications. Each element button over the chart {#ref}1{/ref} adds a 1U application 1s after the last one, and a click on the empty band above the chart adds one at that moment instead. Drag a pill {#ref}2{/ref} to move it, or tap it to change its element, size or time, or to remove it. A focused pill moves with the arrow keys, 0.1s at a time or 1s with Shift. Enter opens its editor, and Delete removes it. {#strong}Clear{/strong} empties the chart, and {#strong}Example scenarios{/strong}, under the chart, loads fourteen examples that each demonstrate an interesting aspect of Genshin’s elemental gauge system.
help_vz_the_chart_draws_each_aura_s_gaug: The chart draws each aura’s gauge over time. Over each application are the reactions it triggered {#ref}3{/ref}, and what it did to its own aura where that matters (topped up, refreshed, or too weak to attach). Beside each drop in a curve {#ref}4{/ref} is what the reaction took off it. Point at the chart and the headline reads the aura on the target at that moment; press to pin the moment, which is how to read one on touch. With nothing pointed at, the headline says when the target is left bare.
help_vz_the_model_is_based_on_kqm_s_stud: The model is based on KQM’s study of Genshin’s elemental gauge, checked against gcsim and stepped at 60 frames a second. An aura keeps 80% of what was applied and decays over 2.5s per unit plus 7s. Applying the same element tops the gauge up but keeps the first application’s decay rate, except Pyro since version 3.0, where a weaker hit does nothing and a stronger one replaces the aura outright. Reactions consume different amounts: forward Vaporize and Melt take twice the trigger, reverse half; Overloaded, Superconduct and Quicken one for one; Swirl and Crystallize half, with a 1s cooldown on Crystallize. Bloom takes Dendro at half the rate of Hydro. Electro-Charged leaves both auras in place and drains each by 0.4U a second. Aggravate and Spread consume nothing.
help_vz_the_instrument_is_built_assuming: The instrument is built assuming one target, and every application you place applies. (ICD is the ICD timeline’s job.) Swirl’s spread to other enemies and Shatter aren’t modeled. Neither are Lunar-Charged, which drains both auras about half as fast as Electro-Charged, or Lunar-Crystallize, which has no cooldown. The other Lunar and Stellar reactions consume the gauge the same way as the reactions they replace.
help_vz_the_icd_timeline_with_hits_every: The ICD timeline with hits every 0.5s under Standard ICD: 2 of every 5 hits apply Electro, bracketed over the first five, with the Hits, Counter, and Timer lanes, and the chart of how often the element lands at each interval beneath.
help_vz_which_hits_in_a_string_actually_: Which hits in a string actually apply their element. The headline is the share that do: for evenly spaced hits, the pattern that repeats in every timer window (“2 of every 5”, bracketed over its hits on the chart {#ref}1{/ref}), and for an example, its whole list. The chart has three lanes on one time axis. In {#strong}Hits{/strong}, a tall stem in the element’s color applies and a short, faint tick is blocked. {#strong}Counter{/strong} is the hit counter, ringed where the counter let a hit through {#ref}2{/ref}. {#strong}Timer{/strong} shows the timer windows, each with how many hits it applied. Point at a hit to read why it did or didn’t apply.
help_vz_the_row_over_the_chart_picks_the: The row over the chart picks the string: evenly spaced hits, or one of four real examples from gcsim (Fischl’s Oz, Hu Tao’s charged attacks, Chevreuse’s burst, and Layla’s Shooting Stars). For evenly spaced hits, the handle under the chart sets the interval, and the strip along it {#ref}3{/ref} shows how often the element lands at every interval: sometimes a slower string lands it more often. Under the chart, {#strong}ICD{/strong} sets the rule: {#strong}Standard{/strong}, {#strong}No ICD{/strong}, or the example’s own fill in its timer, hit counter, and limit per window, and moving any of them makes it {#strong}Custom{/strong}.
help_vz_standard_icd_is_a_2_5s_timer_and: Standard ICD is a 2.5s timer and every third hit, and it stops after eight applications in one window, though no real string gets that far. A hit let through by the timer restarts the timer and the counter; a hit let through by the counter restarts neither. The examples show how far real rules differ: Under its own rule Oz applies on its 1st, 5th and 7th ticks, not the 1st, 4th, 7th and 10th that Standard ICD would allow.
help_vz_send_to_gauge_explorer_hands_the: {#strong}Send to gauge explorer{/strong} hands the first eight applying hits within 15s to the gauge explorer, at 1U each.
help_vz_reaction_curves_with_all_familie: Reaction curves with All families at 600 EM: Transformative leads at +369%, with the next 100 EM drawn as a step on its curve and in the strip under the chart.
help_vz_how_each_family_of_reactions_sca: How each family of reactions scales with Elemental Mastery. The tabs over the chart are the families: Amplifying, Transformative, Additive, Lunar & Stellar, and Crystallize, plus {#strong}All families{/strong}, which puts them on one scale as the bonus each gets from EM. Drag across the chart or the handle under it to set EM. Each curve’s dot shows its value there, and the headline shows what the next 100 EM would add to one of them. What the next 100 EM adds is also visualized as a step on the active curve {#ref}1{/ref} and in the strip under the chart {#ref}2{/ref}. Pick the curve in the bar over the chart, or click its label.
help_vz_every_curve_has_the_same_shape_a: Every curve has the same shape, a bonus of k × EM / (c + EM), with its own k and c per family, and Reaction Bonus adds inside it. The Reaction Bonus setting says how much EM the bonus is worth on the curve you’re reading, which varies a lot: at 600 EM, +40% is worth about 87 EM for a transformative reaction and over 500 for an amplifying one. Level matters for the reactions that scale with it. The level slider runs to 90, then jumps to 95 and 100.
help_vz_every_figure_is_before_the_enemy: Every figure is before the enemy’s RES. Lunar and Stellar reactions show the share of the character who contributes most, 60%. Stellar Swirl’s figures come from gcsim and haven’t been confirmed in game.
help_vz_damage_breakdown_for_a_direct_hi: Damage breakdown for a direct hit at 70% CRIT Rate and 140% CRIT DMG: columns for Scaling ATK, DMG Bonus, Crit, Enemy DEF, and Enemy RES, ending at ×4.28, with gold marks over the crit column.
help_vz_one_hit_written_out_as_its_damag: One hit written out as its damage formula, one column per bracket in the formula’s order, headed by the substat whose next roll would add the most {#ref}1{/ref}. Each bar starts where the last one ended, on a scale where each gridline doubles the damage, so a ×2 is the same size wherever it falls and a cut like enemy DEF runs the other way. Hover or tap a column to read what share of the result it accounts for. Where the tile is narrow, the columns become rows.
help_vz_the_tabs_choose_the_kind_of_hit_: The tabs choose the kind of hit: a direct hit, an additive one like Spread, a transformative reaction, or a Lunar or Stellar one. Set the reaction, your stats, your level, and the enemy in the bar over the chart; only the stats that feed that formula are offered. A column one stat sets, like DMG Bonus or EM, has a grip {#ref}2{/ref}: drag it to change that stat. A direct hit ends as a ratio against a hit from your scaling stat alone, because the talent multiplier isn’t an input. The reaction families end in a number. Enemy RES is entered after shred.
help_vz_the_marks_at_the_end_of_a_bar_ar: The marks at the end of a bar are one more average 5★ roll of each substat that feeds it, as long as what the roll would add, so marks on different bars compare directly; the best is gold {#ref}3{/ref}. DMG Bonus has none, since it can’t appear as an artifact substat. For an additive reaction the gain is measured on the added damage alone, not the whole hit.
help_vz_enemy_res_def_for_pyro_with_viri: Enemy RES & DEF for Pyro, with Viridescent Venerer’s 40% as an arrow along the RES chart landing at ×1.150 and Mavuika’s 20% along the DEF chart landing at ×0.543.
help_vz_how_much_of_a_hit_gets_through_t: How much of a hit gets through the enemy’s resistance and defense, and what your shred adds to it, which is the headline. The RES chart and the DEF chart share one scale: how much of the hit is kept. Drag across the RES chart or the handle under it to set the enemy’s RES, or pick a common value beside the handle. Each source of shred you pick is a segment of the arrow along its chart’s axis, {#ref}1{/ref} and its dot {#ref}2{/ref} shows where you land.
help_vz_shred_works_at_three_strengths_b: Shred works at three strengths. Between 0% and 75% RES it counts in full; below 0% it still helps but at half strength; above 75% it helps but less than in full. Equal levels with the enemy already halve your damage through DEF, and DEF shred and DEF ignore win it back, multiplying together, so the DEF chart counts them as one figure: how much of the enemy’s DEF is gone. Transformative, Lunar, and Stellar reactions ignore DEF entirely; set that with DEF in the bar over the chart.
help_vz_the_shred_setting_holds_every_ch: The Shred setting holds every character and artifact set that shreds the element you’ve chosen, with the constellation it needs and its amounts where they vary. Several shreds add up, but two routes to the same in-game debuff count only once. An immune enemy takes no damage of that element, regardless of the shred.
help_vz_artifact_odds_your_piece_view_fo: Artifact odds’ Your piece view for a +20 flower with CRIT Rate 10.5, CRIT DMG 21.0, ATK% 9.9, and ER 6.5: better than 95% of +20 flowers with these four substats, its 42 CV marked among 100 dots.
help_vz_a_5_artifact_s_odds_over_its_lif: A 5★ artifact’s odds over its life, in four views. Throughout, {#strong}Valued stats{/strong} are the substats you’d count as good. With only CRIT Rate and CRIT DMG valued, results are in crit value; otherwise in useful rolls, where a top roll counts 1 and the smallest 0.7.
help_vz_drop_answers_how_long_a_piece_ta: {#strong}Drop{/strong} answers how long a piece takes to farm. Pick the piece type, every main stat you’d accept, and how many of your valued stats it needs, and the chart shows the chance you’d have it after each day of resin, from the domain alone and during a Stygian Onslaught Outbreak. A day is 180 resin, and a run averages a little over one 5★.
help_vz_level_up_shows_the_chance_a_fres: {#strong}Level up{/strong} shows the chance a fresh piece ends above each value at +20, with 100 dots under the curve, one for each hundredth of the pieces. Drag the chart, or type a value under it, to set the value to beat. It covers pieces that drop with three substats or four, and pieces made with Sanctifying Elixir, which guarantees two of your chosen substats at least two upgrades.
help_vz_your_piece_is_where_you_enter_a_: {#strong}Your piece{/strong} is where you enter a real artifact and see how it measures up. Open it from the toolbar {#ref}1{/ref} and type each substat and its value, or pick them from the list: a field takes only values the game can produce. A badge shows how many upgrades a substat has taken, and when the values fit more than one count, the card asks which one the game shows. Below +20, the chart shows the chance it ends above a value; at +20, the piece is ranked against every +20 piece with the same four substats {#ref}2{/ref}.
help_vz_the_reshape_view_for_the_same_fl: The Reshape view for the same flower, with CRIT Rate and CRIT DMG selected: the Standard, Advanced, and Decreed curves against its 42 CV, and 100 Standard reshapes as dots.
help_vz_reshape_picks_two_substats_as_th: {#strong}Reshape{/strong} picks two substats, as the game’s reshape screen does, and draws all three kinds (Standard, Advanced and Decreed) against your piece. A reshape keeps each substat’s starting roll and rerolls its upgrades. {#strong}Try a reshape{/strong} rolls one and plays it out, then lights where it landed among the dots.
help_vz_the_reshape_guarantee_is_read_as: The reshape guarantee is read as a top-up: Upgrades land at random, and if the two selected substats would end with fewer upgrades than guaranteed, the last upgrades go to them until they meet it. This is how two independent models interpret it: Genshin Optimizer and SiriYu’s solver. The exact in-game method is not confirmed yet.
help_vz_wish_odds_for_c1_of_a_featured_5: Wish odds for C1 of a featured 5★ from 30 pity with the Radiance counter at 2: a 22.4% chance within 120 pulls, with the C0 and C1 curves and the chance on each pull beneath.
help_vz_how_many_pulls_a_goal_takes_from: How many pulls a goal takes from where you are now. Pick what you’re pulling for — a featured 5★, a featured 4★, the charted weapon, or a 5★ and their weapon together — then set what you have, what you’re aiming for (up to C6 and/or R5), your current pity, and whether you hold a guarantee. The chart shows the chance of reaching each step by every pull count. Drag across it, or use {#strong}Pulls saved{/strong} {#ref}1{/ref}, to read your odds with what you have. Starglitter earned while pulling isn’t counted, since how much you get depends on what you pull.
help_vz_you_win_a_50_50_about_55_of_the_: You win a 50/50 about 55% of the time, Capturing Radiance included: that’s the official rate, and what the chart uses until you set your {#strong}Radiance counter{/strong} {#ref}2{/ref}. With it set, the chart follows the community’s model instead. A hidden counter starts at 1 from version 5.0, goes up by one for each 50/50 you lose and down by one for each you win (a guarantee doesn’t move it), and at 3 your next 50/50 is a Capturing Radiance, which sets it back to 1. {#strong}Find mine{/strong} reads your counter, pity and guarantee from a Paimon.moe export, or works the counter out from the 5★s you list. The model comes from OneBST’s analysis of four million wishes, and no history has been found that breaks it; its one unknown is the chance of a Radiance at 2, where we use 9%.
help_vz_a_featured_4_comes_about_22_of_t: A featured 4★ comes about 22% of the time for each 4★ you pull, and a lost 4★ 50/50 never gives you one of the banner’s featured 4★s. (The rate-up 4★ characters on the banner are excluded from the standard pool temporarily for that banner.)
help_vz_on_the_weapon_banner_a_fate_poin: On the weapon banner, a Fate Point charts the weapon you want; without one it’s 37.5% for each featured weapon and 25% for a standard one.
help_vz_the_pity_curves_are_the_game_s_p: The pity curves are the game’s published rates with the community’s soft-pity measurements, and the model is tested against {#gganalysis}GGanalysis{/gganalysis}: Averages agree to two decimal places, and medians agree exactly.
about_critcalc_app_is_three_tools_for_ge: critcalc.app is three tools for Genshin Impact theorycrafting. Many of Genshin’s mechanics are hard to picture in your head. critcalc’s tools were built by a player who wanted to see them drawn out.
about_the_team_builder_is_a_party_setup_: {#strong}The team builder{/strong} is a party setup screen for Stygian Onslaught, the Spiral Abyss, and your own lineups. Each team shows what it can provide (healing, shields, RES shred, buffs, and more), sourced from the kits at the constellations you own, and what switching out a team member would cost or gain. {#builder}How it works{/builder}
about_the_rotation_planner_turns_a_rotat: {#strong}The rotation planner{/strong} turns a rotation written in KQM notation into a timeline of casts and swaps, cooldowns, buff windows, and the enemy’s aura, timed frame by frame. You can also practice a rotation by playing it back at game speed with audio cues. {#planner}How it works{/planner}
about_the_visualizers_are_eight_small: {#strong}The visualizers{/strong} are eight small instruments, each about one mechanic: crit, elemental gauge, ICD, reaction scaling, the damage formula, enemy RES and DEF, artifact odds, and wish odds. {#visualizers}How they work{/visualizers}
about_each_character_starts_from_genshin: Each character starts from genshin-db’s datamined kit and is then curated by hand. The effects, their conditions, and their constellation gates are written from the kit text, and frame counts are measured against gcsim wherever it has the character.
about_curation_is_uneven_because_some_ki: Curation is uneven, because some kits are much harder to model than others. Where a character isn’t finished, the tools say so rather than guess, and the {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage} shows what the rotation planner draws and what it leaves out.
about_critcalc_is_nate_west_s_project_it: critcalc is Nate West’s project. It is one person’s work rather than a team’s, but it leans heavily on what the community has measured. Corrections are welcome! The {#contribute}Contribute{/contribute} page says how to help.
about_gcsim_the_open_source_combat_simul: {#gcsim}gcsim{/gcsim}, the open-source combat simulator: frame data, tick cadences, ICD groups, targeting, and the reference for the gauge model.
about_keqing_mains_the_notation_the_rota: {#kqm}Keqing Mains{/kqm}: the notation the rotation planner reads, and the theorycrafting conventions the tools follow.
about_genshin_db_the_datamined_kits_ever: {#genshindb}genshin-db{/genshindb}: the datamined kits every character starts from.
about_the_genshin_impact_fandom_wiki_kit: {#fandom}The Genshin Impact Fandom wiki{/fandom}: kit details for newer characters, capability lists, and the artifact and wish rates.
about_lunaris_moe_for_stygian_onslaught_: {#lunaris}Lunaris.moe{/lunaris} for Stygian Onslaught and Spiral Abyss data, and {#stygian}Stygian.moe{/stygian} for cross-checking season dates.
about_gganalysis_which_the_wish_odds: {#gganalysis}GGanalysis{/gganalysis}, which the wish odds visualizer is tested against; and Genshin Optimizer and SiriYu’s reshape solver, the two models behind the artifact odds visualizer’s reading of a reshape.
about_eodgamer_s_crit_heatmap_the_spread: {#eodgamer}EODGamer’s crit heatmap{/eodgamer}, the spreadsheet the crit heatmap grew out of.
about_type_is_ibm_plex_and_bitter_the: Type is IBM Plex and Bitter; the interface icons are Lucide’s. Both are open-licensed.
about_critcalc_is_an_unofficial_fan_proj: critcalc is an unofficial fan project, not affiliated with or endorsed by HoYoverse. Genshin Impact, its characters, and its artwork belong to HoYoverse. critcalc takes no money and shows no ads.
about_the_code_is_licensed_under_the_agp: The code is licensed under the AGPL-3.0, and its {#github}source is on GitHub{/github}. The curated data is licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0. critcalc’s own artwork (the logo, the landing silhouettes, some icons, and the scene) is not covered by either.
changelog_known_gaps_are_at_the_bottom_o: {#gaps}Known gaps{/gaps} are at the bottom of the page. For how far each character’s kit has gotten, see the {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage}.

contribute_reports_go_through_the_feedba: Reports go through the {#feedback}feedback form{/feedback}, which takes bugs, characters that behave differently from the game, ideas, and anything else.
contribute_the_quickest_route_is_report_: The quickest route is {#strong}Report a problem{/strong} in the top bar’s {#strong}?{/strong} menu, which opens the form with a link to what you’re looking at, so I see the same rotation, lineup, or instrument you did. A character’s details card has its own link, {#strong}Something not right with this character?{/strong} It fills in the character and their constellation.
contribute_what_helps_most_is_what_you_e: What helps most is what you expected and what you got instead. For a character, the source helps too: the kit text, a gcsim config, or a combat log from the training dummy.
contribute_before_reporting_a_missing_me: Before reporting a missing mechanic, check the {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage}. A part of a kit the rotation planner leaves out on purpose is listed there with the reason.
contribute_help_the_projects_critcalc_is: Help the projects critcalc is built on
contribute_most_of_what_the_tools_show_w: Most of what the tools show was measured by someone else and given to the community. A correction made in one of these projects reaches every tool built on it, critcalc included:
contribute_gcsim_whose_frame_data_and_ti: {#gcsim}gcsim{/gcsim}, whose frame data and tick cadences the rotation planner is timed from. A character implementation or a bug report there helps directly.
contribute_keqing_mains_which_keeps_the_: {#kqm}Keqing Mains{/kqm}, which keeps the notation, the theorycrafting conventions, and the testing behind them.
contribute_thank_you_for_checking_critca: Thank you for checking! critcalc isn’t in need of financial support right now.
beta_critcalc_may_be_rough_around_the_ed: critcalc may be rough around the edges for a bit. It’s a solo project, and while most things have been worked through, new problems still turn up.
beta_i_ve_only_been_able_to_test_the_sit: I’ve only been able to test the site on the few devices I own, so if something doesn’t look right on yours, {#contribute}I’d like to hear about it{/contribute}.
beta_the_character_data_is_where_i_could: The character data is where I could use the most help. Every kit is curated by hand from the kit text and timed against gcsim’s measured frames wherever gcsim has the character, and where a kit isn’t finished the tools say so instead of guessing. The {#coverage}coverage page{/coverage} shows how far each character has gotten.
beta_that_said_i_don_t_have_all_characte: That said, I don’t have all characters or constellations. Calling all mains! If you see something wrong with a character you know, {#contribute}Contribute{/contribute} says how to report it. {#strong}Report a problem{/strong} in the top bar’s {#strong}?{/strong} menu is the fastest way, because it sends a link to exactly what you were looking at.
beta_any_and_all_help_is_appreciated: Any and all help is appreciated!
beta_what_changes_and_what_stays_the_sam: What changes and what stays the same
beta_the_interface_will_keep_changing_fo: The interface will keep changing for a while, and more features are on the way. Coverage of kits will improve as reports get filed and data gaps are uncovered.
beta_while_that_happens_your_saved_data_: While that happens, your saved data won’t be lost. Everything in your Library stays in your browser through every update. It’s still worth downloading a backup now and then ({#strong}Export…{/strong} in Settings), because clearing your browser’s site data erases it. Settings shows when you last did.
privacy_critcalc_has_no_accounts_and_no_: critcalc has no accounts and no server of its own. What you set up stays in your browser. What leaves your browser is listed below.
privacy_everything_you_create_is_kept_in: Everything you create is kept in this browser, on this device only:
privacy_your_settings_display_human_timi: Your settings: display, Human timing, playback sound, and swap ping.
privacy_your_profiles_each_with_its_name: Your profiles, each with its name, picture, and color, its roster (which characters you own or have wishlisted, and at what constellation), its teams and their loadouts, its rotations and lineups, and which of them is open.
privacy_when_you_last_downloaded_a_backu: When you last downloaded a backup, so Settings can tell you.
privacy_whether_critcalc_has_already_ask: Whether critcalc has already asked your browser to keep its data.
privacy_critcalc_sets_no_cookies_a_backu: critcalc sets no cookies. A backup file from {#settings}Settings{/settings} carries all of it. {#strong}Clear data{/strong} on a profile’s own page clears what it holds: its roster, teams, rotations, and lineups. {#strong}Delete everything{/strong} in Settings removes every profile, the Trash, and your settings from this browser.
privacy_browsers_can_clear_a_site_s_stor: Browsers can clear a site’s storage on their own, for example after a while without a visit. The first time you change a rotation or lineup, critcalc asks your browser to keep this site’s data instead. Firefox shows you a prompt for this; other browsers decide by themselves. Settings shows what your browser answered.
privacy_share_links_when_you_send_one: Share links, when you send one
privacy_a_share_link_carries_what_you_re: A share link carries what you’re sharing inside the link itself: a rotation’s notation with its constellations and loadouts, a lineup’s teams, or one instrument’s settings. Nothing about you is added, and nothing is sent anywhere until you paste the link somewhere.
privacy_the_feedback_form_is_a_google_fo: The feedback form is a Google Form. {#strong}Report a problem{/strong} opens it with some answers already filled in: which tool you were in, a share link to what you were looking at, critcalc’s build, and your browser’s user-agent string, plus the error message if something crashed. Those reach Google when the form opens, and become a report only if you submit it. {#google}Google’s privacy policy{/google} covers the form.
privacy_critcalc_uses_cloudflare_web_ana: critcalc uses Cloudflare Web Analytics to count visits: which pages are viewed, the referring site, the browser and device type, and the country. Cloudflare says it uses no cookies or local storage for this and doesn’t record the query string, so the rotation inside a share link isn’t part of it. Its {#cfaq}Web Analytics FAQ{/cfaq} has the details.
privacy_critcalc_is_served_by_cloudflare: critcalc is served by Cloudflare Pages. Like any web host, Cloudflare handles each request, your IP address included, to deliver the page.
privacy_no_accounts_no_ads_no_third_part: No accounts, no ads, no third-party scripts beyond the analytics above, and no fonts or images loaded from anywhere else. Links to other sites open in a new tab, and those sites’ own policies apply there.
privacy_if_any_of_this_changes_this_page: If any of this changes, this page changes first.
